title: European audiences, Belgian friend Robert Goffin, and Caracas telegram album
summary: Armstrong says audiences warm to the theme song, mentions his Belgian lawyer friend who wrote on jazz and visited him backstage during the war, and describes the scrapbook of telegrams from Caracas.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Do you think European people over there have just feeling they're good, though? Anyway, you're worried about it.

The audience is going to enjoy you and things. The people there come there to hear what we're going to do. And from the moment we hit pale moon shining, you know the theme song, everybody sits right there and relax. And from that first note on, the warmth is there. Yeah. Right there in your country, Belgium. A dear friend of mine, Robert Guffin, he's a big lawyer there. And he wrote a book on frontier of jazz years ago. Where we were born probably, you know. That's how far back Belgium is enjoying good jazz and good music.
I think they have, but do you feel the same way?

He was so deep in that music. The same as I am. So during the Second World War, when he had to come to America to meet our president, to Washington, D.C. He got off the plane in New York. And I was playing at the Paramount Theater. And before he moved to play for Washington, he came and spent two days with Satsang. Backstage, sort of out there, playing tapes. See, now I go to Washington. That's like we're pretty big in California. See? And then, when we went into your country, Caracas, I have an album right now that they presented me, a beautiful album, like a scrapbook. And I kept it home until I got sick and split to Italy. And I received so many telegrams with a nice them all on the wall. And when I got home, she took them down, you know, to go home. Now I'm putting those telegrams in that little album, you know, like that big, beautiful thing. Every telegram that was given to me, and I covered up with sketch tape, the most beautiful thing ever seen.
